**A visually smooth option-price surface can still imply inconsistent prices.** No-arbitrage constraints encode relationships that a valid surface should respect under specified market assumptions. For example, convexity in strike for call prices rules out certain butterfly-arbitrage patterns. Maturity comparisons require attention to discounting, dividends, and the chosen normalized quantity. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.11053)

**Soft constraints penalize violations.** Add loss terms for negative convexity or other forbidden derivatives at sampled points. This can improve behavior but does not guarantee validity everywhere between those points. Penalty weights also trade data fit against constraint pressure.

**Hard constraints restrict the function family.** Use a parameterization, constrained basis, or projection that satisfies specified inequalities by construction. This gives stronger guarantees for those exact constraints, but may restrict flexibility and complicate optimization or boundary handling.

Do not confuse a PDE residual penalty with every static no-arbitrage condition: they encode related but distinct assumptions. Automatic differentiation can calculate derivatives, but a computed derivative is only as meaningful as the model, coordinates, and financial setup used.

Evaluate violations on a dense independent grid, boundary behavior, fit to realistic quotes, and robustness to sparse/noisy data. State which conditions are enforced exactly and which are only encouraged. This is a model-design discussion, not a guarantee that a learned surface supports risk-free trading in a market with costs and execution constraints.

**Technical details and references.**

For European call prices under standard fixed-maturity assumptions, price decreases with strike and is convex in strike: $\partial_K C\le0$, $\partial_{KK}C\ge0$, alongside intrinsic/upper bounds. Calendar constraints require consistent discounting, dividends/forwards, and coordinates; “raw call prices always increase with maturity” is too broad. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.11053)

Use a price parameterization with guaranteed monotone/convex structure, or penalize violations on a dense strike/maturity grid. Soft penalties are easier to add but do not guarantee constraints between grid points. Hard constructions restrict expressiveness and need correct boundary conditions.

Validate implied densities, cross-maturity consistency, repricing error weighted by quote quality, and out-of-range behavior. Fitting an implied-volatility surface accurately at observed quotes alone does not ensure arbitrage-free interpolated prices.
